text: You get a string s and a dictionary of words. Break s into pieces that are dictionary words. Some characters may not fit in any word. Return the smallest number of leftover characters.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — I pick some words from the dictionary and place them inside s. Every character I don't cover counts as one extra, and I want to cover as much as I can. Is that right? A few questions. Can the pieces overlap, or can one character be used twice? Are the dictionary words distinct? And is everything lowercase?
No overlap — each character is used at most once. The words are distinct, and everything is lowercase, a to z.
Are there any constraints on the input size?
The string has one to fifty characters, the dictionary has one to fifty words, and each word is one to fifty letters long.

Okay, so everything is small. That tells me a clean DP is enough — I don't need anything fancy. Let me run through the example. s is leetscode, and the dictionary is leet, code, and leetcode. I take leet at zero to three, and code at five to eight. Only the s at index four is left, so the answer is one. Note that leetcode is in the dictionary, but it never shows up in s as one piece, because the s is in the way. Second example: sayhelloworld, with hello and world. Both words fit, say is left, so the answer is three.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to try every choice at every position: skip this character, or start any word that matches here. That branching recursion can blow up exponentially. But the answer for the rest of the string from position i doesn't depend on how I got to i, so the subproblems repeat — a one-dimensional DP over positions. This problem reminds me of the word-segmentation DP: at each position, try every word that can start or end there. The difference is that a character may be skipped, at a cost of plus one. For the matching, a prefix tree lets me walk forward one character at a time and find every word that starts at a position in one walk. I'll show two versions: a trie with a backward DP, and a simpler hash set with a forward DP.

Here's the plan. Same idea in both: first assume this character is extra, plus one, then try to cover it with a word. One: in version A, dp of i is the fewest extras in the suffix from i; dp of n is zero. Two: from each start, I walk the trie and stop at the first missing child; every word end I pass offers dp of end plus one. Three: version B mirrors it, with dp over prefixes, checking every word that ends at i. One thing worth flagging — I must take the min over every word that matches. A short word and a long word can both match at the same spot, so first match wins is wrong. In the trie walk, I only break when a child is missing. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. First, version A, the trie with a backward DP. Each start sets dp to the next cell plus one, then walks from the root. The inner loop breaks only when the child is missing; when is-word is true, I update the min and keep walking, so a longer word can still match. Now version B, the hash set with a forward DP. One thing worth flagging — two code-review notes on B. The set is only looped over; I never call find on it, so it gives no speed-up over looping on the dictionary directly. And string w copies each word on every pass, while substr allocates a new string; a const reference and compare avoid both.

Let's dry-run version A on leetscode. Expected: one. The row that matters is start zero. The walk hits leet, so dp of zero drops to dp of four, which is one. Then the next character is s, and the leet node has no s child, so it breaks — leetcode is never reached, which is correct, since it isn't in s. That's sixteen inner-loop steps. Version B on the same string ends with dp of nine equal to one, after fourteen comparisons, so both versions agree. Corner cases: example two, sayhelloworld, gives three in both. And s equals a b, with dictionary a and a b, gives zero — exactly where breaking on the first word would wrongly give one.

Let me think about complexity here. For version A, building the trie is linear in the total word length, plus n times the longest word for the DP, since each walk stops at the first missing child. For version B, it's n times m times L, where m is the dictionary size, because each comparison costs up to L. Space is twenty-six times the total word length for the trie in A, or just the total word length for the set in B, plus n for dp. In the worst case, with many long words, B pays for every word at every position, while A only follows letters that exist in the trie. With every limit at fifty, both pass easily. Oh, one more thing — version A never frees its trie nodes. That's fine on LeetCode, but in real code I'd use unique pointers or a node pool.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You framed both versions with one rule: assume the character is extra, then try to cover it. You flagged that the first matching word is not enough, and you must take the min over all matches. And you reviewed your own set version honestly: the set is never looked up, the loop copies each word, and compare beats substr. Good work.
